To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) cosine similarity performs poorly in comparison with correlational measures on our data; (ii) the correlational measures are not language-specific; and (iii) a method for extending the correlational approach to inter-language similarity scoring is described and tested.
the most accurate similarity measures are the correlational measures and that the most accurate correlational measure is tetrachoric r.

(1) the cosine similarity measure is a poor predictor of inter-text similarity in any of the five languages studied; (2) the tetrachoric correlational measure is the best predictor of inter-text dissimilarity in all five languages; and (3) the tetrichoric correlation measure can be used to estimate the inter-text dissimiliarity between documents from different languages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question: how similar are two texts?
the calibration and benchmarking of text similarity measures, and with their use for inter-text similarity-scanning across languages.
a fundamental question in linguistic computing, i.e. how can we measure the similarity or dissimilarities between texts?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most reliable method for measuring inter-text similarity in a given corpus is to use a correlational measure on the basis of a human judgement scale.
the best measure of similarity is not cosine similarity, but rather the tetrachoric coefficient of correlation.

, in the absence of a priori knowledge of the texts being compared, the most reliable measure of inter-text similarity is the tetrachoric correlational measure, which outperforms all others on our data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human judgement-based approach to similarity scoring can be extended across language boundaries, and that the results are sufficiently robust to allow the development of a standard for inter-document dissimilarity across languages.
we have developed a method of quantifying the similarity between texts, based on human ratings of similarity, and we have used this to show that widely used measures are inadequate for the task.

we have developed a benchmarking corpus for inter-text similarity-scoping and that the results of our benchmarking study indicate that some widely used similarity measures may be inappropriate for this purpose, and that the use of anchor texts can be a useful way to overcome the problem of cross-language similarity measurement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human judgement of inter-text similarity is a valid and important external benchmark for the evaluation of computational similarity metrics.
similarity indices derived from computational text processing need to be benchmarked against external measures of inter-text similarity if we are to have any confidence in their accuracy.

the use of human judgement to calibrate similarity indices can be a valuable resource in linguistic computing, especially in areas of research such as authorship attribution and plagiarism detection where there are no clear external criteria for measuring the success of the techniques used.
